wds:books.theme: What we owe the crowns we never asked for
wds:books.title: Book One: The Ashen Crown

wds:chapters.content:
The last of the royal fleet burned on the horizon, and Wren watched it from the servants' stair, counting masts the way her mother had taught her to count sheep — one for grief, two for anger, three for the plan that hadn't come yet.

She had four hundred words of that plan and no ending.

wds:characterTemplates.description: The character everyone assumes will die first — survives through intelligence, adaptability, and sheer refusal to break, not raw power.

fields.appearance: Visually contrasts their environment — smaller, paler, or more elegant than the people around them; one distinctive symbolic trait.
fields.arc: From underestimated and dismissed to impossible to ignore — without power ever replacing who they fundamentally are.
fields.backstory: A psychological wound and a social status that explain exactly why everyone underestimates them.
fields.externalConflict: A world that has already decided they're a liability, and waits for them to fail or die first.
fields.fear: Becoming as monstrous as the world they're forced to survive in.
fields.goals: Survive an environment built for people stronger than them, without losing who they are.
fields.internalConflict: Staying emotionally human — compassionate, loyal, afraid — while being pushed into increasingly violent circumstances.
fields.motivations: Prove that intelligence and endurance matter as much as raw strength — and protect the people who see past their reputation.
fields.personality: Sharp, observant, quietly defiant. Compassionate but capable of terrifying resolve when cornered.
fields.strengths: Observation, strategy, pattern recognition, emotional intelligence, creativity under pressure — wins fights indirectly (poison, traps, terrain, exploiting arrogance).
fields.voice: Dry humor and sharp internal observations hide real fear; constantly thinking three moves ahead.
fields.weaknesses: A genuine physical disadvantage that never fully disappears (chronic illness, small stature, lack of training, a trauma-based limitation, etc).

wds:characterTemplates.name: The Intellectual Underdog Protagonist

sections.body:
"The character everyone assumes will die first… who survives through intelligence, adaptability, emotional resilience, and sheer refusal to break."

This protagonist is not the strongest, fastest, richest, or most naturally gifted fighter.
They survive because:
- They think faster than others.
- They adapt under pressure.
- They weaponize perceived weakness.
- They refuse to surrender emotionally.
- They endure pain better than people expect.
sections.title: Core Archetype

sections.body:
The world sees them as:
- Weak
- Frail
- Unsuitable
- Too soft
- Too intelligent for a brutal environment
- A liability
- Someone protected by privilege/family reputation
- Someone who doesn't belong

The protagonist knows:
- Some of this is true.
- Most people underestimate them.
- Underestimation is useful.
sections.title: Character Foundation — Public Identity

sections.body:
The best underdog protagonists are built around contradiction.

External Trait → Internal Truth
- Physically weak → Mentally relentless
- Emotionally compassionate → Capable of terrifying violence when cornered
- Intelligent/bookish → Learns combat through adaptation
- Afraid → Still acts
- Socially overlooked → Eventually becomes impossible to ignore
sections.title: The Core Contradiction

sections.body:
1. Physical Disadvantage
Give them a genuine disadvantage that cannot simply disappear.
Examples: chronic illness, small stature, injury-prone body, lack of formal training, lower social class, late entry into an elite institution, trauma-induced limitation, magical deficiency, physical disability.
The key: the disadvantage must remain relevant even after they grow stronger. (Violet's fragility never truly disappears.)

2. Intelligence as Survival
The protagonist wins through observation, preparation, strategy, pattern recognition, emotional intelligence, manipulation when necessary, creativity under pressure.
They should often defeat stronger opponents indirectly — poison, traps, psychological warfare, political maneuvering, exploiting arrogance, using terrain/environment.

3. Emotional Core
Core emotional traits: compassion, loyalty, empathy, protective instincts, fear of losing loved ones, desire to prove themselves, survivor's guilt, fear of becoming monstrous.
This creates tension: they are forced into increasingly violent worlds while trying not to lose themselves.

4. Defiance
The underdog needs moments where they refuse to submit despite overwhelming odds — not because they think they'll win, but because their pride refuses surrender, someone weaker needs protection, their moral code demands action, or they'd rather die than become cowardly. These moments create audience attachment.
sections.title: Essential Underdog Traits

sections.body:
Internal Monologue Style
Use: sharp observations, dry humor, self-awareness, fear hidden beneath sarcasm, constant tactical thinking.
Avoid: endless self-pity, passive reactions, excessive whining.
sections.title: Character Voice

sections.body:
Underdog protagonists often visually contrast their environment.
Examples: smaller silhouette among soldiers, pale/sickly appearance in warrior culture, elegant features in a brutal setting, visible scars/braces/wrappings, a distinctive symbolic trait (silver hair, strange eyes, ritual marks).
The goal: make them visually memorable while appearing vulnerable.
sections.title: Visual Design

sections.body:
Choose 1–2 major flaws.
Good Underdog Flaws: recklessness when loved ones are threatened, refusal to ask for help, self-sacrificial tendencies, stubbornness, emotional avoidance, trust issues, desire to prove themselves, fear of weakness, mercy toward dangerous enemies.
sections.title: Fatal Flaw Options

sections.body:
The protagonist cannot become interesting because they become powerful.
They become interesting because: they suffer, they adapt, they persist, they remain emotionally human while surviving inhuman circumstances.
Power is only meaningful if it threatens to change who they are.

sections.title: Quick Build Template

wds:characterTemplates.description: Inspired by the "dangerous protector with hidden softness" archetype (Xaden Riorson, Fourth Wing) — feared by everyone except the one person he lets in.

fields.appearance: "Beautiful enough to be dangerous" — dark clothing, scars, sharp features, predatory stillness.
fields.arc: From controlled and untouchable to devastatingly gentle with exactly one person, without ever fully losing his edge.
fields.backstory: A war, betrayal, or forced leadership that taught him survival requires emotional suppression.
fields.externalConflict: A reputation as a monster/weapon that he never bothers to correct, even when it costs him.
fields.fear: That loving someone openly will get them killed — or reveal how much he needs them.
fields.goals: Keep control of everything and everyone around him so no one else he loves gets taken from him.
fields.internalConflict: Wants peace and connection but was raised to believe love is a liability.
fields.motivations: Protect the people (or person) he's claimed, whatever the cost to himself.
fields.personality: Ruthless and untouchable on the outside; loyal, exhausted, and quietly lonely underneath.
fields.secrets: The rumors about him are only partly true — he never corrects the rest.
fields.strengths: Overwhelming competence — combat, strategy, leadership, reading people; makes difficult things look effortless.
fields.trauma: Learned early that love leads to loss; responsibility was forced on him before he was ready.
fields.voice: Short sentences, dry humor, controlled intensity — rare emotional admissions that land hard because they're so rare.
fields.weaknesses: Emotional repression, self-sacrificial to a fault, terrified that attachment is what gets people killed.

wds:characterTemplates.name: The Dangerous Love Interest

sections.body:
A male love interest template inspired by Fourth Wing character Xaden Riorson — built around the "dangerous protector with hidden softness" archetype.

"The man everyone fears… who becomes devastatingly gentle with only one person."

This character is: powerful, emotionally guarded, highly competent, morally gray, dangerous to everyone except the protagonist.
But underneath: he carries enormous guilt, he protects people through sacrifice, he secretly wants peace more than violence, love terrifies him because attachment creates weakness.
sections.title: Core Archetype

sections.body:
The appeal of this archetype comes from contradiction.

External Persona → Internal Reality
- Ruthless → Deeply loyal
- Emotionally cold → Feels everything intensely
- Feared leader → Exhausted protector
- Violent → Selectively gentle
- Untouchable → Secretly lonely
- In control → One emotional trigger away from collapse
sections.title: The Core Fantasy

sections.body:
The world sees him as: a monster, a weapon, a killer, a war hero, untouchable, dangerous, morally corrupt, the last person anyone should trust.

Rumors about him should circulate constantly, e.g.:
- "He killed someone during initiation."
- "He's never lost a fight."
- "He executes traitors personally."
- "He enjoys violence."
- "He's incapable of love."
Some rumors are true. Some are exaggerated. He never corrects them.
sections.title: Character Foundation — Public Reputation

sections.body:
1. Competence
This archetype must feel overwhelmingly capable — combat, strategy, leadership, reading people, manipulation, survival, crisis management. The key: he makes difficult things look effortless. Competence creates attraction before romance even begins.

2. Emotional Restraint
He rarely shows vulnerability openly. Emotion leaks through actions — protection replaces confession, sacrifice replaces vulnerability, physical closeness replaces emotional honesty.
Examples: standing guard outside her door, quietly patching wounds, remembering tiny details, watching exits automatically, positioning himself between danger and others.

3. Controlled Violence
Violence is part of his identity, but he uses it surgically and never loses control publicly. His rage becomes frightening because it is usually restrained. Important: he should feel dangerous even when calm.

4. Buried Softness
The softness must exist beneath layers of discipline. Soft moments should feel rare and earned — dry humor, protective gestures, quiet intimacy, exhaustion slipping through, unexpected tenderness, gentle physical contact, revealing personal rituals or scars. This contrast is the emotional payoff.
sections.title: Essential Traits

sections.body:
This archetype works best when he learned early that love leads to loss, responsibility was forced onto him too young, and survival required emotional suppression.
Common backstory elements: failed rebellion, war orphan, betrayal, political hostage, dead family, forced leadership, childhood violence, burden of protecting others.
sections.title: The Traumatized Protector Formula

sections.body:
This is the emotional center of the archetype.
Everyone else gets: coldness, discipline, intimidation, distance.
The protagonist gets: patience, honesty, protection, vulnerability, emotional attention.
The shift should happen gradually.
sections.title: The "Only Soft For Them" Dynamic

sections.body:
With the Underdog Protagonist
The love interest initially underestimates them, or becomes fascinated immediately. Then realizes: they are emotionally dangerous to him, he cares too much, their survival affects his decisions. This terrifies him.

Why He Falls In Love
He doesn't fall for beauty alone. He falls because the protagonist challenges him, sees through him, refuses to fear him, makes him want to become better, survives despite impossible odds, understands loneliness, treats him like a human instead of a weapon.
sections.title: Relationship Dynamics

sections.body:
The visual goal: "Beautiful enough to be dangerous."
Common design elements: dark clothing, scars, tattoos/relics/marks, large silhouette, sharp features, intense eye contact, predatory stillness, elegant violence, black leather / military aesthetic, a distinct symbolic weapon.
Xaden's visual identity emphasizes shadows, scars, dark clothing, and lethal composure.
sections.title: Visual Design

sections.body:
Dialogue Style
Use: short sentences, dry humor, controlled intensity, teasing dominance, strategic honesty, rare emotional admissions.
Examples of tone: "Careful." / "You're staring." / "That's a terrible idea." / "Stay behind me." / "You're safer with me." / "I said I'd protect you."
sections.title: Character Voice

sections.body:
The Mask (what people see): ruthless, unfeeling, cold, arrogant, violent.
The Real Person (what the protagonist slowly discovers): exhausted, lonely, loyal to a fault, secretly compassionate, terrified of failure, self-sacrificial.
The romance works because the protagonist becomes one of the few people allowed behind the mask.
sections.title: The Mask vs. The Real Person

sections.body: This archetype should not be morally clean. He should lie when necessary, kill without hesitation, manipulate strategically, break rules, commit morally questionable acts for survival. But he has lines he refuses to cross — his morality is rooted in protection, loyalty, and survival.
sections.title: The Moral Grayness

sections.body: Choose 2–3: emotional repression, self-sacrificial behavior, obsessive protectiveness, trust issues, ruthlessness, martyr complex, belief he is unlovable, difficulty communicating, extreme independence, anger issues hidden beneath composure, need for control.
sections.title: Fatal Flaws

sections.body:
Every version of this archetype needs a deep internal wound. Examples:
- "Everyone I love dies."
- "I am becoming the monster I hate."
- "My usefulness is the only reason people keep me."
- "If people truly knew me, they'd fear me."
- "I was raised to be a weapon, not a person."
This wound should drive most of his choices.
sections.title: The Secret Wound

sections.body:
The relationship becomes compelling when the protagonist emotionally destabilizes him, he physically protects them, and they emotionally humanize him — both save each other differently.
He protects their body. They protect his soul.
sections.title: The Power Dynamic

sections.body: The character should not just be "hot because he's dangerous." He becomes compelling because he carries unbearable responsibility, hides pain behind control, love forces him to become emotionally vulnerable, and the protagonist makes him want to live instead of merely survive.

sections.title: Quick Build Template

wds:characterTemplates.description: Inspired by Dain Aetos — a morally rigid, system-loyal antagonist who hurts the protagonist by loving them incorrectly, not by hating them.

fields.arc: Either admits they were wrong and chooses the protagonist over the system (redemption), or doubles down and becomes what they feared (tragic fall).
fields.backstory: Once the protagonist's emotional safe place — a friendship built long before it curdled into control.
fields.beliefs: Rules and order are the only things standing between the world and catastrophe.
fields.externalConflict: The protagonist keeps outgrowing the protection the antagonist insists on giving them.
fields.fear: Chaos — losing people, losing control, being powerless to stop disaster.
fields.goals: Maintain order and protect the people they love, even if it means overriding those people's choices.
fields.internalConflict: Genuinely loves the protagonist but is loyal to systems over people when the two conflict.
fields.motivations: Keep the protagonist (and the world) safe by keeping them controlled, protected, and inside the rules.
fields.personality: Disciplined, dependable, rule-bound — genuinely convinced they know what's best for the protagonist.
fields.strengths: Discipline, leadership, social trust — respected by authority figures for following the system without hesitation.
fields.trauma: A childhood built on conditional love and pressure to perform, where usefulness became identity.
fields.voice: Controlled, rational, protectively worded — dangerous because they always sound reasonable.
fields.weaknesses: Cannot accept the protagonist's growth; mistakes control for love.

wds:characterTemplates.name: The Antagonist — Misguided Protector

sections.body:
A morally complex antagonist template inspired by Dain Aetos — built around control, loyalty to systems, emotional intimacy with the protagonist, and the tragedy of becoming the obstacle instead of the protector.

"The person who genuinely believes they are protecting the protagonist… while slowly destroying their trust, freedom, and identity."

This antagonist is not: pure evil, sadistic, chaotic, power-hungry in an obvious way.
Instead, they are: loyal to order, emotionally attached to the protagonist, morally rigid, terrified of losing control, convinced they know what's best.
The tragedy: they hurt the protagonist because they love them incorrectly.
sections.title: Core Archetype

sections.body:
External Persona → Internal Reality
- Dependable → Emotionally controlling
- Protective → Deeply insecure
- Morally upright → Capable of violating trust
- Loyal → Loyal to systems over people
- Caring → Unable to truly listen
- Safe → Emotionally dangerous
sections.title: The Core Contradiction

sections.body:
This archetype becomes compelling when their intentions are understandable, their methods become unforgivable, and they never fully realize the damage until too late.
The audience should constantly feel: "If they had trusted the protagonist instead of controlling them, none of this would've happened."
sections.title: The "Misguided Protector" Formula

sections.body:
The world sees them as: reliable, disciplined, honorable, responsible, leadership material, a model soldier/student/heir, someone people should trust.
Authority figures love them because they follow rules, value stability, obey systems, and make difficult choices without hesitation.
Unlike chaotic antagonists, this character is socially respected.
sections.title: Character Foundation — Public Reputation

sections.body:
At the center of this archetype is usually fear of chaos.
Examples: fear of losing people, fear of disorder, fear of rebellion, fear of emotional unpredictability, fear of becoming powerless, fear of failing their duty, fear that love will destroy objectivity.
This fear drives their need for control, rules, structure, surveillance, certainty.
sections.title: The Core Fear

sections.body:
1. Genuine Care
The audience must believe: "They really do care about the protagonist." Without this, they become a generic antagonist. They should worry constantly, try to protect the protagonist, remember small details, show emotional history, be unable to let go emotionally. The problem: their care becomes suffocating.

2. Moral Rigidity
This character believes rules exist for survival, order prevents catastrophe, personal feelings cannot override duty. They often say things like: "There are reasons these rules exist." / "You don't understand the bigger picture." / "I'm trying to protect you." / "You're being reckless." / "Someone has to think rationally."

3. Infantilization Of The Protagonist
They cannot emotionally accept the protagonist's growth. They continue seeing them as fragile, naive, vulnerable, in need of protection — even after the protagonist proves themselves repeatedly. This becomes emotionally infuriating because the antagonist loves an outdated version of the protagonist. (Dain's conflict with Violet heavily stems from his inability to stop viewing her as fragile despite her growth and survival.)

4. The "Crossed A Line" Moment
This archetype requires one major violation of trust — invading privacy, reporting the protagonist, choosing authority over friendship, revealing secrets, betraying confidence, making decisions for them, sacrificing someone "for the greater good." The key: they justify it completely at first.
sections.title: Essential Traits

sections.body:
This archetype often represents institutions, tradition, militarism, religion, political order, authority structures.
They are dangerous because they genuinely believe the system is morally correct — even when the system is corrupt, the protagonist suffers under it, and innocent people die.
sections.title: The System-Loyal Antagonist

sections.body:
This antagonist is strongest when they were once the protagonist's emotional safe place, they know the protagonist intimately, and they slowly become emotionally incompatible.
The audience mourns who they used to be together. (Dain's emotional impact comes largely from being Violet's childhood best friend before becoming someone she can no longer fully trust.)
sections.title: The Emotional Tragedy

sections.body:
This archetype often exists as a foil.
The Antagonist Represents: safety, stability, rules, familiarity, predictability, approved choices.
The Love Interest Represents: freedom, risk, emotional truth, growth, rebellion, transformation.
The protagonist choosing the love interest symbolizes choosing self-actualization over safety.
sections.title: The Foil to the Love Interest

sections.body:
With The Protagonist
The antagonist often thinks they know the protagonist best, believes they understand what's good for them, becomes frustrated when ignored, feels replaced emotionally, resents losing influence.
Their emotional arc becomes: "Why won't you trust me anymore?" — without realizing they destroyed trust themselves.
sections.title: Relationship Dynamics

sections.body: Scene Types: emotional arguments disguised as concern; "I'm doing this for your own good"; rule-versus-morality conflicts; forced betrayals; watching the protagonist choose someone else; discovering they were wrong too late; realizing authority manipulated them; failed attempts at reconciliation; protectiveness becoming possessiveness; quiet regret after irreversible damage.
sections.title: The Best Scenes For This Archetype

sections.body:
Dialogue Style
Use: controlled language, rational explanations, emotional restraint, protective wording, frustrated concern.
Examples: "Think for one second." / "I'm trying to keep you alive." / "You're acting emotionally." / "This isn't about trust." / "You don't understand what's at stake." / "I did what I had to do."
Their tone becomes dangerous because they sound reasonable.
sections.title: Character Voice

sections.body:
The visual goal: "Trusted authority figure hiding emotional instability."
Common elements: clean uniform/clothing, precise grooming, structured silhouette, military/academic aesthetic, controlled posture, warm eyes with tense expressions, subtle signs of exhaustion beneath perfection.
Unlike chaotic villains, their appearance communicates control.
sections.title: Visual Design

sections.body:
This archetype usually has a foundational wound tied to conditional love, pressure to perform, fear of failure, parental expectations, emotional repression, identity built around usefulness.
Examples: "If I stop being useful, I become worthless." / "Rules are the only thing keeping the world from collapsing." / "Love makes people weak." / "If I lose control, people die." / "Duty matters more than feelings."
sections.title: The Secret Wound

sections.body: Choose 2–3: need for control, moral rigidity, inability to adapt, emotional repression, fear of uncertainty, blind trust in authority, jealousy, possessiveness disguised as protection, inability to admit wrongdoing, viewing vulnerability as weakness, savior complex.
sections.title: Fatal Flaws

sections.body:
This archetype works best when they eventually face the horrifying realization: "I became part of the thing I thought I was protecting people from." This creates two paths.

Redemption Path: they admit they were wrong, break from authority, choose the protagonist over the system, accept consequences, learn to trust instead of control. (Dain's later arc increasingly centers around guilt, shattered faith in authority, and attempts to repair the damage he caused.)

Tragic Fall Path: they double down, refuse accountability, become increasingly authoritarian, lose the protagonist permanently, become what they once feared. Most tragic version: they realize the truth too late to fix anything.
sections.title: The Fall Or Redemption

sections.body: This antagonist should make readers feel angry, frustrated, sympathetic, heartbroken — sometimes simultaneously. Because the real emotional pain comes from watching someone who loves the protagonist become incapable of truly seeing them anymore.

sections.title: Quick Build Template

sections.body: Why this archetype works: villains who hate the protagonist are predictable. But someone who loves the protagonist while hurting them creates emotional devastation.
sections.title: The Emotional Formula

wds:characterTemplates.description: A once-real friendship that fractures under fear, ideology, jealousy, or duty — the betrayal that hurts because the love was real.

fields.arc: Either seeks forgiveness and redemption, or lets pride keep them from reconciliation even though both still care.
fields.backstory: A real, earned friendship — inside jokes, shared history, mutual survival — that makes the eventual betrayal feel personal, not villainous.
fields.externalConflict: A breaking point (ideological, fear-driven, jealous, protective, or corrupting) that outside pressure pushes them past.
fields.fear: Being left behind, replaced, or proven irrelevant as the protagonist grows beyond them.
fields.goals: Before the break: stand by the protagonist no matter what. After: justify why they didn't.
fields.internalConflict: Still loves the protagonist even while betraying them — and knows it.
fields.motivations: Depends on the betrayal type chosen: ideology, fear, jealousy, protection, or slow corruption.
fields.personality: Warm, funny, emotionally open — the kind of friend the protagonist never thought to doubt.
fields.secrets: A resentment or fear they never said out loud until it was too late.
fields.strengths: Emotional accessibility and real history with the protagonist — they know exactly how to comfort them, and later, exactly how to hurt them.
fields.voice: Before: easy teasing and comforting honesty. After: sharper, more formal — notably, they stop using the protagonist's nickname.
fields.weaknesses: Fear of abandonment, need for validation, or blind loyalty to authority — whichever fuels their eventual breaking point.

wds:characterTemplates.name: The Betrayer Best Friend

sections.body:
A best-friend-turned-betrayer template inspired by the emotional role characters like Rhiannon Matthias and Dain Aetos play in The Empyrean series — built around loyalty, emotional intimacy, fractured trust, and devastating ideological conflict.

"The person who knew the protagonist best… and became the one capable of hurting them most."

This character is not evil. That's what makes the betrayal devastating.
They are: loyal, loving, protective, deeply bonded to the protagonist.
But eventually fear, ideology, jealousy, duty, survival, resentment, or love itself pushes them into betrayal.
The audience should think: "I understand why they did it… but it still hurts."
sections.title: Core Archetype

sections.body:
The betrayer works because they once represented safety, the protagonist trusted them completely, and their betrayal feels emotionally intimate.
This archetype is strongest when the betrayal feels PERSONAL rather than villainous.
sections.title: The Core Emotional Formula

sections.body:
Before betrayal, the friendship must feel real. The best friend should defend the protagonist early, help them survive, share secrets, train/study/work together, develop rituals and inside jokes, become emotionally dependable.
The reader must genuinely believe: "These two would die for each other."
sections.title: The Foundation of the Friendship

sections.body:
External Role → Internal Conflict
- Loyal friend → Growing resentment
- Supportive ally → Feels abandoned
- Moral compass → Secretly compromised
- Protector → Capable of betrayal
- Trusted confidant → Hiding dangerous truths
sections.title: The Core Contradiction

sections.body:
Choose the emotional flavor carefully.

1. The Ideological Betrayal — they believe the protagonist is wrong, duty outweighs friendship, the system matters more than personal loyalty. The "I thought I was saving you" betrayal.

2. The Fear Betrayal — they're terrified, the consequences feel too large, survival instincts override loyalty. Most realistic version.

3. The Jealousy Betrayal — the protagonist changes while they remain stagnant; they begin feeling left behind, replaced, inferior, invisible. Especially effective when the protagonist gains power/status/romance and the friendship becomes emotionally imbalanced.

4. The Protective Betrayal — they betray because they think "This is the only way to save you." Usually tragic rather than malicious.

5. The Slow Corruption Betrayal — the character gradually changes through power, trauma, manipulation, political pressure, forbidden magic, obsession. The protagonist notices too late.
sections.title: Types of Betrayal

sections.body:
1. Genuine Loyalty (At First)
The betrayal only works if the loyalty was once real. The friendship cannot be fake from the beginning. They should save the protagonist, defend them publicly, know personal vulnerabilities, provide emotional stability. The betrayal hurts because the love was real.

2. Emotional Accessibility
Unlike colder characters, this archetype is emotionally open — they talk easily, joke often, show affection naturally, express emotion openly, feel approachable and human. This creates contrast with later emotional distance.

3. Moral Conviction
The betrayer should believe they are justified. Even at their worst, they rationalize their actions morally, believe the protagonist forced their hand, see themselves as necessary. The audience should occasionally agree with them.

4. Lingering Love
Even after betrayal, they still care, they hesitate, they regret things, they try to justify themselves, they still know the protagonist intimately. This makes scenes emotionally volatile.
sections.title: Essential Traits

sections.body:
The betrayal should attack trust, emotional intimacy, vulnerability — not just physical safety.
The best betrayal moments include lines like:
- "I did this for you."
- "You left me behind."

wds:characters.arc: From a girl following her mother's rules to a ruler who writes her own.
wds:characters.backstory: Escaped the palace the night it fell, hidden by a servant who died getting her out.
wds:characters.externalConflict: Every house that could help her also wants her dead.
wds:characters.fear: Becoming the kind of ruler her father was.
wds:characters.goals: Unite the fractured houses under a single banner before the dying god wakes.
wds:characters.internalConflict: Wants to be loved as a person, not obeyed as a crown.
wds:characters.motivations: Reclaim the crown to protect the people her family failed.
wds:characters.name: Wren Ashmark
wds:characters.personality: Controlled on the outside, furious underneath. Plans three moves ahead and hates that she has to.
quotes: "I have counted every mast on that horizon. I intend to make them count me back."

relationships.notes: She does not trust him for the first third of the book, on purpose.

wds:characters.voice: Formal in public, dry and sharp in private.
wds:characters.weaknesses: Struggles to trust anyone who wasn't staff in the palace.

wds:characters.appearance: A scar through one eyebrow from the job that made him quit.
wds:characters.arc: From a man who kills kings for coin to one who dies, if it comes to it, protecting one.
wds:characters.motivations: Atone for the crowns he's already helped topple.
wds:characters.name: Kael Vantry
wds:characters.personality: Charming as armor. Funnier the more scared he actually is.
quotes: "I was hired to end a princess. Turns out I'm better at the opposite work."

relationships.notes: Slow-burn — starts as employer/hired blade, becomes something neither of them planned.

wds:characters.arc: Either seeks forgiveness and redemption, or lets pride keep them from reconciliation even though both still care.
wds:characters.backstory: A real, earned friendship — inside jokes, shared history, mutual survival — that makes the eventual betrayal feel personal, not villainous.
wds:characters.externalConflict: A breaking point (ideological, fear-driven, jealous, protective, or corrupting) that outside pressure pushes them past.
wds:characters.fear: Being left behind, replaced, or proven irrelevant as the protagonist grows beyond them.
wds:characters.goals: Before the break: stand by the protagonist no matter what. After: justify why they didn't.

wds:documents.notes:
THE INTELLECTUAL UNDERDOG PROTAGONIST TEMPLATE





Core Archetype
“The character everyone assumes will die first… who survives through intelligence, adaptability, emotional resilience, and sheer refusal to break.”
This protagonist is not the strongest, fastest, richest, or most naturally gifted fighter.
They survive because:
They think faster than others.
They adapt under pressure.
They weaponize perceived weakness.
They refuse to surrender emotionally.
They endure pain better than people expect.

CHARACTER FOUNDATION
Public Identity
The world sees them as:
Weak
Frail
Unsuitable
Too soft
Too intelligent for a brutal environment
A liability
Someone protected by privilege/family reputation
Someone who doesn’t belong
The protagonist knows:
Some of this is true.
Most people underestimate them.
Underestimation is useful.

THE CORE CONTRADICTION
The best underdog protagonists are built around contradiction.

External Trait
Internal Truth
Physically weak
Mentally relentless
Emotionally compassionate
Capable of terrifying violence when cornered
Intelligent/bookish
Learns combat through adaptation
Afraid
Still acts
Socially overlooked
Eventually becomes impossible to ignore






ESSENTIAL UNDERDOG TRAITS
1. Physical Disadvantage
Give them a genuine disadvantage that cannot simply disappear.
Examples:
Chronic illness
Small stature
Injury-prone body
Lack of formal training
Lower social class
Late entry into elite institution
Trauma-induced limitation
Magical deficiency
Physical disability
The key:
The disadvantage must remain relevant even after they grow stronger.
Violet’s fragility never truly disappears.

2. Intelligence as Survival
The protagonist wins through:
Observation
Preparation
Strategy
Pattern recognition
Emotional intelligence
Manipulation when necessary
Creativity under pressure
They should often defeat stronger opponents indirectly.
Examples:
Poison
Traps
Psychological warfare
Political maneuvering
Exploiting arrogance
Using terrain/environment

3. Emotional Core
Underdogs become compelling when they remain emotionally human despite brutal environments.
Core emotional traits:
Compassion
Loyalty
Empathy
Protective instincts
Fear of losing loved ones
Desire to prove themselves
Survivor’s guilt
Fear of becoming monstrous
This creates tension:
They are forced into increasingly violent worlds while trying not to lose themselves.

4. Defiance
The underdog needs moments where they refuse to submit despite overwhelming odds.
Not because they think they’ll win.
Because:
Their pride refuses surrender.
Someone weaker needs protection.
Their moral code demands action.
They would rather die than become cowardly.
These moments create audience attachment.




CHARACTER VOICE
Internal Monologue Style
Use:
Sharp observations
Dry humor
Self-awareness
Fear hidden beneath sarcasm
Constant tactical thinking
Avoid:
Endless self-pity
Passive reactions
Excessive whining

VISUAL DESIGN
Underdog protagonists often visually contrast their environment.
Examples:
Smaller silhouette among soldiers
Pale/sickly appearance in warrior culture
Elegant features in brutal setting
Visible scars/braces/wrappings
Distinctive symbolic trait (silver hair, strange eyes, ritual marks)
The goal:
Make them visually memorable while appearing vulnerable.

FATAL FLAW OPTIONS
Choose 1–2 major flaws.
Good Underdog Flaws:
Recklessness when loved ones are threatened
Refusal to ask for help
Self-sacrificial tendencies
Stubbornness
Emotional avoidance
Trust issues
Desire to prove themselves
Fear of weakness
Mercy toward dangerous enemies

THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE
The protagonist cannot become interesting because they become powerful.
They become interesting because:
They suffer.
They adapt.
They persist.
They remain emotionally human while surviving inhuman circumstances.
Power is only meaningful if it threatens to change who they are.

wds:documents.notes:
DANGEROUS LOVE INTEREST TEMPLATE




A male love interest template inspired by Fourth Wing character Xaden Riorson — built around the “dangerous protector with hidden softness” archetype.

Core Archetype
“The man everyone fears… who becomes devastatingly gentle with only one person.”
This character is:
Powerful
Emotionally guarded
Highly competent
Morally gray
Dangerous to everyone except the protagonist
But underneath:
He carries enormous guilt.
He protects people through sacrifice.
He secretly wants peace more than violence.
Love terrifies him because attachment creates weakness.

THE CORE FANTASY
The appeal of this archetype comes from contradiction:

External Persona
Internal Reality
Ruthless
Deeply loyal
Emotionally cold
Feels everything intensely
Feared leader
Exhausted protector
Violent
Selectively gentle
Untouchable
Secretly lonely
In control
One emotional trigger away from collapse







CHARACTER FOUNDATION
Public Reputation
The world sees him as:
A monster
A weapon
A killer
A war hero
Untouchable
Dangerous
Morally corrupt
The last person anyone should trust
Rumors about him should circulate constantly.
Examples:
“He killed someone during initiation.”
“He’s never lost a fight.”
“He executes traitors personally.”
“He enjoys violence.”
“He’s incapable of love.”
Some rumors are true.
 Some are exaggerated.
 He never corrects them.

ESSENTIAL TRAITS
1. Competence
This archetype must feel overwhelmingly capable.
He should excel at:
Combat
Strategy
Leadership
Reading people
Manipulation
Survival
Crisis management
The key:
He makes difficult things look effortless.
Competence creates attraction before romance even begins.

2. Emotional Restraint
He rarely shows vulnerability openly.
Instead:
Emotion leaks through actions.
Protection replaces confession.
Sacrifice replaces vulnerability.
Physical closeness replaces emotional honesty.
Examples:
Standing guard outside her door
Quietly patching wounds
Remembering tiny details
Watching exits automatically
Positioning himself between danger and others

3. Controlled Violence
Violence is part of his identity.
But:
He uses it surgically.
He never loses control publicly.
His rage becomes frightening because it is usually restrained.
Important:
He should feel dangerous even when calm.

4. Buried Softness
The softness must exist beneath layers of discipline.
Soft moments should feel rare and earned.
Examples:
Dry humor
Protective gestures
Quiet intimacy
Exhaustion slipping through
Unexpected tenderness
Gentle physical contact
Revealing personal rituals or scars
This contrast is the emotional payoff.

THE TRAUMATIZED PROTECTOR FORMULA
This archetype works best when:
He learned early that love leads to loss.
Responsibility was forced onto him too young.
Survival required emotional suppression.
Common backstory elements:
Failed rebellion
War orphan
Betrayal
Political hostage
Dead family
Forced leadership
Childhood violence
Burden of protecting others


THE “ONLY SOFT FOR THEM” DYNAMIC
This is the emotional center of the archetype.
Everyone else gets:
Coldness
Discipline
Intimidation
Distance
The protagonist gets:
Patience
Honesty
Protection
Vulnerability
Emotional attention
The shift should happen gradually.

RELATIONSHIP DYNAMICS
With the Underdog Protagonist
The love interest initially:
Underestimates them
 OR
Becomes fascinated immediately
Then realizes:
They are emotionally dangerous to him.
He cares too much.
Their survival affects his decisions.
This terrifies him.

Why He Falls In Love
He doesn’t fall for beauty alone.
He falls because the protagonist:
Challenges him
Sees through him
Refuses to fear him
Makes him want to become better
Survives despite impossible odds
Understands loneliness
Treats him like a human instead of a weapon



VISUAL DESIGN
The visual goal:
“Beautiful enough to be dangerous.”
Common design elements:
Dark clothing
Scars
Tattoos/relics/marks
Large silhouette
Sharp features
Intense eye contact
Predatory stillness
Elegant violence
Black leather / military aesthetic
Distinct symbolic weapon
Xaden’s visual identity emphasizes shadows, scars, dark clothing, and lethal composure.

CHARACTER VOICE
Dialogue Style
Use:
Short sentences
Dry humor
Controlled intensity
Teasing dominance
Strategic honesty
Rare emotional admissions
Examples of tone:
“Careful.”
“You’re staring.”
“That’s a terrible idea.”
“Stay behind me.”
“You’re safer with me.”
“I said I’d protect you.”

THE MASK VS THE REAL PERSON
The Mask
What people see:
Ruthless
Unfeeling
Cold
Arrogant
Violent
The Real Person
What the protagonist slowly discovers:
Exhausted
Lonely
Loyal to a fault
Secretly compassionate
Terrified of failure
Self-sacrificial
The romance works because:
The protagonist becomes one of the few people allowed behind the mask.

THE MORAL GRAYNESS
This archetype should not be morally clean.
He should:
Lie when necessary
Kill without hesitation
Manipulate strategically
Break rules
Commit morally questionable acts for survival
But:
He has lines he refuses to cross.
His morality is rooted in protection, loyalty, and survival.

FATAL FLAWS
Choose 2–3:
Emotional repression
Self-sacrificial behavior
Obsessive protectiveness
Trust issues
Ruthlessness
Martyr complex
Belief he is unlovable
Difficulty communicating
Extreme independence
Anger issues hidden beneath composure
Need for control

THE SECRET WOUND
Every version of this archetype needs a deep internal wound.
Examples:
“Everyone I love dies.”
“I am becoming the monster I hate.”
“My usefulness is the only reason people keep me.”
“If people truly knew me, they’d fear me.”
“I was raised to be a weapon, not a person.”
This wound should drive most of his choices.

THE POWER DYNAMIC
The relationship becomes compelling when:
The protagonist emotionally destabilizes him.
He physically protects them.
They emotionally humanize him.
Both save each other differently.
He protects their body.
 They protect his soul.



THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE
The character should not just be:
“Hot because he’s dangerous.”
He becomes compelling because:
He carries unbearable responsibility.
He hides pain behind control.
Love forces him to become emotionally vulnerable.
The protagonist makes him want to live instead of merely survive.

wds:sections.body:
A best-friend-turned-betrayer template inspired by the emotional role characters like Rhiannon Matthias and Dain Aetos play in The Empyrean series — built around loyalty, emotional intimacy, fractured trust, and devastating ideological conflict.

"The person who knew the protagonist best… and became the one capable of hurting them most."

This character is not evil. That's what makes the betrayal devastating.
They are: loyal, loving, protective, deeply bonded to the protagonist.
But eventually fear, ideology, jealousy, duty, survival, resentment, or love itself pushes them into betrayal.
The audience should think: "I understand why they did it… but it still hurts."
wds:sections.title: Core Archetype

wds:sections.body:
The betrayer works because they once represented safety, the protagonist trusted them completely, and their betrayal feels emotionally intimate.
This archetype is strongest when the betrayal feels PERSONAL rather than villainous.
wds:sections.title: The Core Emotional Formula

wds:sections.body:
Before betrayal, the friendship must feel real. The best friend should defend the protagonist early, help them survive, share secrets, train/study/work together, develop rituals and inside jokes, become emotionally dependable.
The reader must genuinely believe: "These two would die for each other."
wds:sections.title: The Foundation of the Friendship

wds:sections.body:
External Role → Internal Conflict
- Loyal friend → Growing resentment
- Supportive ally → Feels abandoned
- Moral compass → Secretly compromised
- Protector → Capable of betrayal
- Trusted confidant → Hiding dangerous truths
wds:sections.title: The Core Contradiction

wds:sections.body:
Choose the emotional flavor carefully.

1. The Ideological Betrayal — they believe the protagonist is wrong, duty outweighs friendship, the system matters more than personal loyalty. The "I thought I was saving you" betrayal.

2. The Fear Betrayal — they're terrified, the consequences feel too large, survival instincts override loyalty. Most realistic version.

3. The Jealousy Betrayal — the protagonist changes while they remain stagnant; they begin feeling left behind, replaced, inferior, invisible. Especially effective when the protagonist gains power/status/romance and the friendship becomes emotionally imbalanced.

4. The Protective Betrayal — they betray because they think "This is the only way to save you." Usually tragic rather than malicious.

5. The Slow Corruption Betrayal — the character gradually changes through power, trauma, manipulation, political pressure, forbidden magic, obsession. The protagonist notices too late.
wds:sections.title: Types of Betrayal

wds:sections.body:
1. Genuine Loyalty (At First)
The betrayal only works if the loyalty was once real. The friendship cannot be fake from the beginning. They should save the protagonist, defend them publicly, know personal vulnerabilities, provide emotional stability. The betrayal hurts because the love was real.

2. Emotional Accessibility
Unlike colder characters, this archetype is emotionally open — they talk easily, joke often, show affection naturally, express emotion openly, feel approachable and human. This creates contrast with later emotional distance.

3. Moral Conviction
The betrayer should believe they are justified. Even at their worst, they rationalize their actions morally, believe the protagonist forced their hand, see themselves as necessary. The audience should occasionally agree with them.

4. Lingering Love
Even after betrayal, they still care, they hesitate, they regret things, they try to justify themselves, they still know the protagonist intimately. This makes scenes emotionally volatile.
wds:sections.title: Essential Traits

wds:sections.body:
The betrayal should attack trust, emotional intimacy, vulnerability — not just physical safety.
The best betrayal moments include lines like:
- "I did this for you."
- "You left me behind."
- "You stopped trusting me first."
- "I had no choice."
- "You were becoming someone I didn't recognize."
- "I still love you."
- "I thought I was saving everyone."
